claims.text: Hypercalcemia by level: oral phosphate for calcium < 11.5 mg/dL with mild symptoms and no kidney disease; IV saline and furosemide for faster correction below 18 mg/dL; bisphosphonates or other calcium-lowering drugs for 11.5 to 18 mg/dL and/or moderate symptoms; hemodialysis above 18 mg/dL
claims.quote: Oral phosphate for serum calcium < 11.5 mg/dL (< 2.9 mmol/L) with mild symptoms and no kidney disease IV saline and furosemide for more rapid correction of elevated serum calcium < 18 mg/dL (< 4.5 mmol/L) Bisphosphonates or other calcium-lowering medications for serum calcium 11.5 to 18 mg/dL (3.7 to 5.8 mmol/L) and/or moderate symptoms Hemodialysis for serum calcium >18 mg/dL (> 5.8 mmol/L)

claims.text: Saline volume repletion: an essential part of care; the rest depends on the degree and cause of the hypercalcemia
claims.quote: The treatment used depends on both the degree and the cause of hypercalcemia. Volume repletion with saline is an essential element of care.

claims.text: Saline plus a loop diuretic: 1 to 2 L of saline over 2 to 4 hours (unless significant heart failure), then furosemide 20 to 40 mg IV every 2 to 4 hours as needed for urine output of about 250 mL/hour; check K and Mg as often as every 4 hours; calcium falls to near-normal within 24 hours
claims.quote: Another treatment is increasing urinary calcium excretion by giving isotonic saline plus a loop diuretic. Initially, 1 to 2 L of saline is given over 2 to 4 hours unless significant heart failure is present because nearly all patients with significant hypercalcemia are hypovolemic. Furosemide 20 to 40 mg IV every 2 to 4 hours is given as needed to maintain a urine output of roughly 250 mL/hour (monitored hourly). Care must be taken to avoid volume depletion. Potassium and magnesium are monitored as often as every 4 hours during treatment and replaced IV as needed to avoid hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. Serum calcium begins to decrease in 2 to 4 hours and falls to near-normal within 24 hours.

claims.text: Bisphosphonates: usually the drugs of choice for cancer-associated hypercalcemia; zoledronic acid 4 mg IV once lowers calcium for an average of > 40 days
claims.quote: Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclasts. They are usually the medications of choice for cancer-associated hypercalcemia. Zoledronic acid can be given as a one-time dose of 4 mg IV and lowers serum calcium very effectively for an average of > 40 days.

claims.text: Calcitonin: salmon calcitonin 4 to 8 IU/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours lowers calcium by 1 to 2 mg/dL within a few hours, but tachyphylaxis often sets in after about 48 hours
claims.quote: A salmon calcitonin dosage of 4 to 8 IU/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours is safe. Calcitonin can lower serum calcium levels by 1 to 2 mg/dL within a few hours. Its usefulness in the treatment of cancer-associated hypercalcemia is limited by its short duration of action with the development of tachyphylaxis (often after about 48 hours) and by the lack of response in ≥ 40% of patients.

claims.text: Corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone 20 to 40 mg orally once a day): an adjunct that lowers calcitriol production, for vitamin D toxicity and sarcoidosis
claims.quote: Corticosteroids (eg, prednisone 20 to 40 mg orally once a day) can help control hypercalcemia as adjunctive therapy by decreasing calcitriol production and thus intestinal calcium absorption in most patients with vitamin D toxicity, idiopathic hypercalcemia of infancy, and sarcoidosis.

claims.text: Severe hypercalcemia (> 18 mg/dL or severe symptoms): hemodialysis with low-calcium dialysate may be needed on top of other treatments
claims.quote: In severe hypercalcemia (serum calcium > 18 mg/dL [> 4.5 mmol/L] or with severe symptoms), hemodialysis with low-calcium dialysate may be needed in addition to other treatments.

claims.text: Hypercalcemia of malignancy: saline first (with or without furosemide); denosumab or an IV bisphosphonate if fluids don't work; add calcitonin if still unresponsive; hemodialysis if the others fail
claims.quote: Saline (with or without furosemide, depending on volume status) may be used as initial treatment. Denosumab or an IV bisphosphonate is generally needed if hypercalcemia does not respond to fluid administration. Calcitonin can be added if hypercalcemia remains unresponsive. Hemodialysis is needed to lower calcium level acutely if other treatments are not successful
claims.locator: Treatment of Hypercalcemia, Hypercalcemia of malignancy

claims.text: Hypocalcemic tetany: calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% solution IV over 10 minutes; the response may last only a few hours, so repeat boluses or an infusion (20 to 30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate in 1 L of 5% dextrose over 12 to 24 hours) may be needed
claims.quote: For tetany, calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% solution IV over 10 minutes is given. Response can be dramatic but may last for only a few hours. Repeated boluses or a continuous infusion with 20 to 30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate in 1 L of 5% dextrose in water over the next 12 to 24 hours may be needed.

claims.text: IV calcium with digoxin: hazardous; give slowly with continuous ECG monitoring, after checking for and correcting hypokalemia
claims.quote: Infusions of calcium are hazardous in patients receiving digoxin and should be given slowly and with continuous ECG monitoring after checking for (and correcting) hypokalemia.

claims.text: Tetany with low magnesium: calcium or potassium helps only briefly; it is relieved for good only by repleting magnesium
claims.quote: When hypocalcemic tetany is also associated with hypomagnesemia, it may respond transiently to calcium or potassium administration but is permanently relieved only by repletion of magnesium

claims.text: Chronic hypocalcemia: oral calcium, 1 to 2 g of elemental calcium a day, and occasionally vitamin D (e.g., cholecalciferol 800 IU once a day if no renal failure or hypoparathyroidism)
claims.quote: In chronic hypocalcemia, oral calcium and occasionally vitamin D supplements are usually sufficient: 1 to 2 g of elemental calcium/day may be given as calcium gluconate or calcium carbonate. In patients without renal failure or hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D is given as a standard oral supplement (eg, vitamin D3, cholecalciferol, 20 mcg [800 IU] once/day).

claims.text: Renal failure or hypoparathyroidism: use calcitriol (or another vitamin D analog that doesn't need kidney activation); in hypoparathyroidism usually 0.5 to 2 mcg orally once a day
claims.quote: For patients with renal failure, calcitriol or another vitamin D analog that does not require renal metabolic alteration (eg, alfacalcidiol, dihydrotachysterol) should be used. Patients with hypoparathyroidism also have difficulty converting cholecalciferol to its active form and also often require calcitriol, usually 0.5 to 2 mcg orally once a day.

claims.text: When to treat low magnesium: when symptomatic or persistently < 1.25 mg/dL; patients with alcohol use disorder are treated empirically
claims.quote: Treatment with magnesium salts is indicated when magnesium deficiency is symptomatic or the magnesium concentration is persistently < 1.25 mg/dL (< 0.50 mmol/L). Patients with alcohol use disorder are treated empirically.

claims.text: Oral magnesium: e.g., magnesium gluconate 500 to 1000 mg 3 times a day for 3 to 4 days; diarrhea limits oral treatment
claims.quote: In practice, oral magnesium salts (eg, magnesium gluconate 500 to 1000 mg orally 3 times a day) are given for 3 to 4 days. Further boluses are given until the serum magnesium level has normalized. Oral treatment is limited by the onset of diarrhea.

claims.text: Severe symptomatic hypomagnesemia (e.g., seizures): 2 to 4 g of magnesium sulfate IV over 5 to 10 minutes
claims.quote: In severe, symptomatic hypomagnesemia (eg, magnesium < 1.25 mg/dL [< 0.5 mmol/L] with seizures or other severe symptoms), 2 to 4 g of magnesium sulfate IV is given over 5 to 10 minutes.

claims.text: Low magnesium with low K or Ca: address those too, but they are hard to correct until magnesium is repleted
claims.quote: Concurrent hypokalemia or hypocalcemia should be specifically addressed in addition to hypomagnesemia. These electrolyte disturbances are difficult to correct until magnesium has been repleted.

claims.text: Treat the cause of low phosphate: e.g., stop phosphate-binding antacids or diuretics, or correct hypomagnesemia
claims.quote: Removal of the cause of hypophosphatemia may include stopping phosphate-binding antacids or diuretics or correcting hypomagnesemia.

claims.text: Oral phosphate: with treatment of the cause, usually enough in asymptomatic patients even when the level is very low; up to about 1 g 3 times a day
claims.quote: Treatment of the underlying disorder and oral phosphate replacement are usually adequate in asymptomatic patients, even when the serum concentration is very low. Phosphate can be given in doses up to about 1 g orally 3 times a day in tablets containing sodium phosphate or potassium phosphate.

claims.text: IV phosphate: when phosphate is < 1 mg/dL, with rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis or CNS symptoms, or when oral replacement isn't feasible
claims.quote: Parenteral phosphate is usually given IV. It should be administered in any of the following circumstances: When serum phosphate is < 1 mg/dL (< 0.32 mmol/L) Rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, or central nervous system symptoms are present Oral replacement is not feasible due to the underlying disorder

claims.text: IV phosphate pace: usually no more than 7 mg/kg over 6 hours; faster rates risk hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia and metastatic calcification
claims.quote: In most cases, no more than 7 mg/kg (about 500 mg for a 70-kg adult) of phosphate should be given over 6 hours. Close monitoring is done, and more rapid rates of phosphate administration should be avoided to prevent hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and metastatic calcification due to excessive calcium phosphate product.

claims.text: On insulin or a sulfonylurea: plasma glucose < 70 mg/dL counts as hypoglycemia and should be treated
claims.quote: In patients treated with glucose-lowering medications (insulin or sulfonylureas), a plasma glucose level < 70 mg/dL (< 3.9 mmol/L) is considered hypoglycemia and should be treated to avoid further decreases in blood glucose and consequences of hypoglycemia.

claims.text: Rule of 15s: take 15 g of glucose or sucrose, recheck in 15 minutes, and take another 15 g if glucose is not > 80 mg/dL; once > 80 mg/dL, a snack with complex carbohydrates and protein
claims.quote: The rule of 15s should be followed for treatment of hypoglycemia. Typically, 15 g of glucose or sucrose should be ingested. Patients should check their glucose levels 15 minutes after glucose or sucrose ingestion and ingest an additional 15 g if their glucose level is not > 80 mg/dL (> 4.4 mmol/L). After glucose levels improve to > 80 mg/dL, a snack containing complex carbohydrates and protein may be ingested to prevent the glucose level from dropping again.

claims.text: Unable to eat or drink: glucagon 1 mg (0.5 mg if < 25 kg) subcutaneously or IM, or glucagon nasal spray 3 mg in 1 nostril
claims.quote: Adults and children who are unable to eat or drink can be given glucagon 0.5 mg (< 25 kg body weight) or 1 mg (≥ 25 kg) subcutaneously or intramuscularly. Glucagon nasal spray, 1 actuation (3 mg) once in 1 nostril may be used in adults and in children ≥ 4 years.

claims.text: Hospitalized adults: 50% dextrose, 50 to 100 mL IV bolus, with or without a 5 to 10% dextrose infusion until symptoms resolve
claims.quote: Adults or adolescents who are hospitalized can be treated with 50% dextrose, 50 to 100 mL IV bolus, with or without a continuous infusion of 5 to 10% dextrose solution until symptoms resolve.

claims.text: Glucagon needs liver glycogen: it has little effect after prolonged fasting or prolonged hypoglycemia
claims.quote: The efficacy of glucagon depends on the size of hepatic glycogen stores; glucagon has little effect on plasma glucose in patients who have been fasting or who are hypoglycemic for long periods.

claims.text: Prolonged or severe hypoglycemia: admit for continuous IV dextrose; with sulfonylurea ingestion, give octreotide along with dextrose
claims.quote: Patients with prolonged or severe hypoglycemia should be hospitalized for continuous intravenous dextrose infusion. In cases of severe hypoglycemia due to sulfonylurea ingestion, octreotide should be administered along with dextrose.
